Review
Promoting Mis/Disinformation Literacy Among Adults: A Scoping Review of Interventions and Recommendations
Megan Bolerhttps://orcid.org/0000-0003-2379-46351, Hoda Gharib1, Yoon-Ji Kweon2, Amanda Trigiani1, and Barbara Perry3
Abstract
This scoping review contributes an overview of recent research on effective media literacy interventions and recommendations relevant to cultivating critical mis/disinformation literacies for adults. The review examines articles published between 1 January 2016–22 November 2021 that report on or provide recommendations for media literacy interventions for adults suited to the emerging challenges of disinformation. Our findings reveal diverse intervention formats and evaluation methods including course-, web-, or game-based interventions, public events, and visual resources. Experts recommended teaching about emotion targeting and regulation, algorithmic governance, lateral reading, visual technology, and using interactive formats. Studies of evaluated interventions outside of formal education were scarce. Our review reveals significant debates around the usefulness of checklists and how to address politically sensitive issues, skepticism, and authority in programing. Future research and programing must attend to the needs of adult populations outside of formal education, and draw particularly upon librarians’ integral role in delivering community-based mis/disinformation literacy programing.
Keywords
social media, topics, political polarization, topics, problematic internet use, topics, news and newsworthiness, topics, knowledge sharing, topics
1OISE/University of Toronto, Toronto, ON, Canada
2University of Toronto, Toronto, ON, Canada
3Ontario Tech University, Oshawa, ON, Canada
Corresponding author(s):
Megan Boler, OISE/University of Toronto, 252 Bloor Street West, Toronto, ON M5S 1A1, Canada. Email: megan.boler@utoronto.ca
Introduction
While dis- and misinformation are by no means new phenomena, their increasing sophistication and proliferation pose an intractable challenge in our modern technologically driven societies. As false information is produced and spread with greater speed and more volume than ever before, distinguishing true from false information is increasingly difficult (Roozenbeek & Van Der Linden, 2019). Technology that allows for the production of “deepfakes” (Westerlund, 2019), the capture of user data for political and/or economic gain (Boler & Davis, 2021), and the production of misleading content at scale through artificial intelligence (Kreps et al., 2022) have facilitated the conditions for a societal “truth decay” and declining trust in the press and governmental institutions (Freelon & Wells, 2020; Hameleers, 2023; Kavanagh & Rich, 2018). “Problematic information” (Jack, 2017) – which includes fake news, media manipulation, coordinated inauthentic behavior, and propaganda – has exploded with unprecedented vengeance, reflecting a “fundamental shift within the technological and political underpinnings of mediated communication in modern democracies” (Egelhofer & Lecheler, 2019, p. 98).
While the study of propaganda became well established during the interwar period, scholarly focus on mis/disinformation distinctively emerges after the 2016 US presidential election of Donald Trump, as both the actual phenomenon of disinformation, and the weaponized label of “fake news” dominated popular discourse (Chomintra, 2023; Freelon & Wells, 2020; Kapantai et al., 2021; Wright et al., 2023). Scholars distinguish mis- and disinformation by intent: misinformation describes incorrect or misleading information that is unintentionally disseminated, while disinformation includes “false, inaccurate, or misleading information designed, presented and promoted to intentionally cause public harm or for profit” (European Commission, 2018, p. 3).
In addition to this proliferation of false information within the heightened context of global content creation and dissemination, some studies find that older adults are more likely to share disinformation than younger populations (A. Guess et al., 2019). These concerns force educators, librarians, and policymakers, amongst others, to ask: How can we ensure that contemporary media literacy and education practices are up to the challenge of countering mis/disinformation (Boler et al., 2023; Wright et al., 2023)? What practices best address the needs of adults faced with the prevalence of online mis/disinformation (Droog et al., 2024; Dumitru et al., 2022)? Current scholarship tends to draw upon existing understandings of “media literacy” and “information literacy,” which respectively focus on critiquing media messages and on locating accurate information, yet neither has yet to sufficiently take into account new challenges posed by 21st century technologies (Jones-Jang et al., 2021).
Further, while much media literacy research caters to children and youth programing, there is a lack of research and published evaluations of programing for those above 18 years, particularly outside formal education (Bulger & Davison, 2018; Dumitru et al., 2022; Rasi et al., 2021). Rasi et al. (2021) systematic review found only 40 English-language articles reporting on practical media literacy interventions targeting older adults, particularly concerning given these populations are amongst the most vulnerable to mis/disinformation (Brashier & Schacter, 2020). As Lee notes, “fake news, scams, phishing, and other risks. . . often target not children but adults” (Lee, 2018, p. 460), gaps similarly noted in Dumitru et al.’s (2022) systematic review of research between 2010 and 2020.
Our scoping review seeks to address these gaps by supporting research that can inform urgently needed mis/disinformation literacy catered to adults. We examine research and expert recommendations from the unique period of 2016 to 2021, when librarians, scholars, and educators began to recognize the serious threat of mis/disinformation. Indeed, at the time this review was conducted in 2021, the term “disinformation literacy” could be found only in a handful of articles (Al-Musalli, 2022; Courchesne et al., 2021; Hwang et al., 2021;J. P. Roberts, 2022). By 2022, as noted as well by Droog et al. (2024), the topic began to receive intense scholarly attention (see e.g., Chomintra, 2023; Dumitru et al., 2022; Kanozia et al., 2022). Drawing from established definitions (Brisola & Doyle, 2019; European Commission, 2018; Wardle & Derakhshan, 2017) and current debates (Dumitru et al., 2022; Frau-Meigs, 2022; Wright et al., 2023), we understand mis/disinformation literacy as the ability, confidence, and motivation to critically assess information, and to both recognize and reject false, misleading, or manipulated content (including text, audio, and visual). The general ability to detect and discriminate false from true information is distinct from the ability to reject this false information, as identifiably false information that affirms an individual’s biases may be willingly accepted and shared as another form of disinformation (Batailler et al., 2022). Therefore, we attend to both mis- and disinformation detection and rejection as components of comprehensive mis/disinformation literacy. Ideally, mis/disinformation literacy involves understanding the complex (social, political, historical, economic, technological, and cultural) factors shaping the media landscape and the production of information, news, and social media. Finally, mis/disinformation literacy requires critical reflexivity regarding the psychological, emotional, partisan and identity-based motivations that shape our ideologies and beliefs, and render us vulnerable to and also likely to spread (however unintentionally) mis/disinformation.
Our review focuses on mis/disinformation literacy for adults, with the aim of understanding both evidence-based research in the disciplines of social sciences and education during this important and nascent period of mis/disinformation study, as well as expert recommendations (i.e., from librarians and media literacy practitioners) regarding future directions in media literacy research and education for adults.
Our review is guided by two central research questions:
RQ1: What is the current state of research on adult media literacy programing targeting mis/disinformation, particularly within social sciences and education?
RQ2: What recommendations do media literacy interventions and experts provide to effectively promote adult mis/disinformation literacy?
Methods
This scoping review contributes an overview of recent research on effective media literacy interventions and recommendations relevant to cultivating critical mis/disinformation literacies for adults. Based on the preliminary research conducted to develop our funding proposal, a scoping review was best suited to a multidisciplinary exploration of gaps surrounding adult-based, mis/disinformation-focused media literacy. Scoping reviews map relevant research by identifying types of evidence, key concepts, and how research on a given topic tends to be conducted, and include studies that range in methodology. Often used as a “precursor to a systematic review” (Munn et al., 2018, p. 143), scoping reviews tend to be less evaluative and more descriptive than systematic reviews (Pham et al., 2014), aiming more broadly to document the range and nature of the current literature and to “clarify a complex concept and refine subsequent research inquiries” (Levac et al., 2010, p. 1) by identifying knowledge gaps.
Inclusion and Exclusion Criteria
Our inclusion and exclusion criteria were developed in close consultation with University of Toronto librarians with expertise in scoping and systematic reviews, following PRISMA guidelines (Page et al., 2021). Given our interest in research within the social sciences and education, we focused our inquiry on relevant disciplines including psychology, sociology, education, and library sciences. Our search was conducted on November 22, 2021, and included articles that were written in English and published on/after January 1, 2016. The year 2016 was chosen because it reflects the significant turning point of Donald Trump’s election, and resulting increase in the use of the term “fake news” alongside public and scholarly concerns regarding disinformation (Tandoc et al., 2018). Notably, this review documents a moment prior to and during a significant increase in publications exploring the implications of mis/disinformation, most specifically the context of the COVID-19 pandemic, the rise of artificial intelligence, and technologies such as ChatGPT which present an outsized impact and challenge within our media landscape.
We included peer-reviewed articles, commentaries, findings, and recommendations from government, community (e.g., library), and non-research settings. Peer-reviewed articles provide up-to-date discussions and debates on mis/disinformation from experts in the field, as well as evidence-based practices regarding the design and implementation of media literacy programs. We included articles that described interventions, programing, or curricula (hereinafter referred to as “interventions”) that either focused on or were relevant to educating adults on how to engage with and analyze news and information in a critical way and how to recognize and reject mis/disinformation (following Batailler et al., 2022). Studies that described an intervention and its effects or “lessons learned” but did not follow a strictly experimental study design were still included. Following Loss (2008), we understand interventions as any planned and implemented program, curriculum, or activity that aims to change or impact media literacy-related knowledge, attitudes, or behaviors of a person, an organization, or a population.
In light of the glaring gaps, our review includes essays containing recommendations for interventions from librarians and experts relevant to aiding adults in targeting mis/disinformation. This practice follows Levac et al. (2010), who emphasize the value of including findings that “address questions beyond those related to intervention effectiveness, and generate findings that can complement the findings of clinical trials” (p. 1). Although we primarily focused on interventions and recommendations targeting adult populations, we included articles targeting upper-high school students because interventions or recommendations for this population may be transferable both to college-age and adult populations (Hobbs, 2020). We excluded articles if (1) they focused solely on children and not adults or upper high school-aged youth; (2) they were published before January 1, 2016; (3) their full-text was written in a language other than English; (4) they did not discuss media education related interventions or recommendations pertaining to the recognition, evaluation, or engagement with (false) information.
Search Strategy and Screening Procedure
The review was conducted by a large collaborative team including two PIs and five research assistants over 7 months (September 2021–March 2022), and our search strategy was developed through repeated consultation with two University of Toronto (UT) librarians as well as our two disinformation and media literacy expert consultants. Following the advice of the UT librarians, we utilized databases which best targeted our research questions and concerns related to social sciences and education: IBSS, Sociological Abstracts, ERIC, LISA, LISTA, WPSA, PAIS, PsycINFO. Some guidelines suggest that including Google or Google Scholar has limited search functionality and may introduce bias related to personalized algorithms of the user conducting the search, and thus may be less easily replicable (Piasecki et al., 2018; Rethlefsen et al., 2021).
Test versions of the search string were used across all of the databases, developed over a month through four rounds of discussions and reviews held between the research team and librarians to finalize the search string. Adaptation and changes to the search string were made through such processes as: reviewing suggested terms found across the unique databases; consulting with our librarians for additional terms; experimenting with different Boolean operator combinations and proximity searches; consulting database-specific thesauruses.
The finalized searches are shown below. For databases featured on EBSCO, we removed the “NEAR/2” directive and placed quotation marks around the two terms between the brackets. Separate searches were conducted using each search string in all databases. The limits included in the databases are NOFT (anywhere but full text), open to both peer review and other, published in English, and dated January 1, 2016 or after.
DISINFORMATION: disinformation OR misinformation OR propaganda OR (news NEAR/2 fake) OR (conspira* NEAR/2 theor*) OR (information NEAR/2 mislead*) OR (deep NEAR/2 fake*) OR (media NEAR/2 trust) OR (false NEAR/2 information)
MEDIA EDUCATION: (Critical* NEAR/2 litera*) OR (digital* NEAR/2 litera*) OR (media NEAR/2 litera*) OR (information* NEAR/2 litera*) OR (civic* NEAR/2 litera*) OR (news* NEAR/2 litera*) OR (data NEAR/2 litera*) OR (media NEAR/2 educat*) OR (media NEAR/2 curricul*) OR (media NEAR/2 program*) OR (resilien* NEAR/2 citizen*) OR (new NEAR/2 litera*) OR (visual NEAR/2 litera*) OR (“social media” NEAR/2 litera*) OR (metalitera*)
Our screening process involved multiple phases. As a team, we discussed the inclusion/exclusion criteria and search strings over weekly team meetings. We tested iterations of the search strings across the databases and skimmed the resultant abstracts and keywords to determine their relevance to our research questions. Results of more advanced searches were documented and presented to the two expert librarian consultants for feedback.
To test and finalize our selection criteria for the studies, we conducted a pilot review with a test unit of 45 abstracts using Covidence, a commonly used literature review software. All five team members and the PIs reviewed these 45 articles and held discussions until we reached consensus on the inclusion/exclusion criteria.
We then moved to the official process of conducting searches across all databases, which yielded 759 studies for review. These were uploaded into Covidence, which removed duplicates (n = 150), bringing us to 609 studies. Five reviewers sequentially evaluated the titles and abstracts of these publications to determine relevancy, with two reviewers’ approval needed to include each study, leaving 409 studies for full-text review. Five team members reviewed the full text of the articles, with two reviewers each reading approximately 160 articles. We arrived at a list of 227 studies for inclusion in our review (see Appendix). Any disagreements on study selection in the abstract and full-text reviews were resolved by the PIs who reviewed the conflicts and made the final decision (Levac et al., 2010). When reading the final group of articles, reviewers noted details of the publications in an Excel chart according to the following column headings: full citation, sample size, (study) purpose, target population and facilitator, article type and methods, realized interventions, suggested interventions, psychological factors, relevant findings/recommendations, and researcher notes. Findings and recurring themes in the chart were discussed across multiple meetings over the next 2 months.
Findings
Article Characteristics
Publication Timeline and DisciplinesFigure 1 illustrates the number of articles that were published between 2016 and 2021, revealing a sharp increase in publications during 2017 and gradual incline until publications peaking in 2020, with a small decline in 2021. Figure 2 shows a breakdown of disciplines and the number of articles pertaining to each. The largest concentration of the articles returned by our search was from librarian and information sciences journals (n = 112, 49.3%), followed by the field of education (n = 61, 26.8%). While efforts to tackle mis/disinformation have traditionally involved librarians in formal educational settings, this breakdown of articles illustrates librarians’ central role in addressing mis/disinformation literacy:

Figure 1. Number of articles published from 2016 until 2021.

Figure 2. Breakdown of the percentage of articles per discipline.
MethodologiesFigure 3 shows the breakdown of article methodologies. Essays, newsletters, and opinion pieces (36.1%, n = 82) were most prevalent, tending to offer a general review of issues in the information landscape and advocacy for media education. The second most prevalent were overviews of current programing and pedagogies (31.3%, n = 71), which included descriptive case studies, summaries, and suggested approaches to media literacy but lacked formal evaluations of particular approaches. Our corpus also included articles that used correlational and experimental study designs (28.6%; n = 65), of which 21 (9.2%) reported on the results of experimental or field studies. Finally, literature reviews (4.0%, n = 9) systematically identified themes, patterns, and gaps in media literacy research related to mis/disinformation. We were concerned to note that although media literacy interventions present the most useful basis for developing and implementing initiatives against disinformation, they are distinctively underrepresented among extant literature.

Figure 3. Breakdown of articles by methodology.
Target PopulationsFigure 4 visualizes the percentage of articles targeting specific populations in their studies and/or recommendations. The majority were aimed at youth populations in formal education settings (46.7%, n = 106), while the remainder targeted: populations of multiple or unspecified age groups (34.8%, n = 79), librarians and educators (11.0%, n = 25), or adult populations outside formal education (7.5%, I = 17). The articles that aimed at youth catered to students in higher education (26.4%, n = 60), high school (11.0%, n = 25), or to “youth” or “students” of unspecified ages (9.3%, n = 21). The lack of articles focused on adults outside of formal education demonstrates again this glaring gap in disinformation media literacy literature.

Figure 4. Percentage of articles that targeted various populations through their studies and/or recommendations.
Defining Mis/Disinformation-Related Terms
The very concept of disinformation is contested and variously defined across the literature. We did not find an overarching term that encompassed all mis/disinformation threats but instead a variety of related terms. The most prominent term to emerge in our review was “fake news” (81.1%, n = 184), though not without criticism. Hobbs (2017b) noted that “fake news” is too broad to be a useful descriptor, while Head et al. (2018) stated that “fake news” is itself a propaganda strategy given its right-wing appropriation and associations. Faix (2018) stated that “fake news” has “come to be synonymous for any news which the reader doesn’t agree with, doesn’t like, or doesn’t want to acknowledge” (p. 44).
Further, the majority of articles (53.3%, n = 121) did not define the terms they used, and terms such as “fake news,” “misinformation,” “disinformation,” and “false information” were used interchangeably. However, within studies that defined their use of disinformation-related terms, there is extensive discussion on how to differentiate them.
Intentionality is seen as an important marker of distinction between false information-related terms, particularly misinformation and disinformation. Many studies cite Wardle and Derakhshan (2017), who define misinformation as false information shared without the intent of harm, disinformation as false information knowingly shared to cause harm, and mal-information as genuine and often private information shared to cause harm. These concepts were designated as information disorders under the label of fake news (cf. Damasceno, 2021). Alvarez (2021) supported the view that fake news is an umbrella term for mis- and disinformation, but noted that mistakes and malicious intent can be difficult to distinguish, especially when targeted disinformation is unwittingly spread by users who believe it is genuine. When presenting the results of our study in what follows, we use the terms “misinformation” and “disinformation” according to the language used and definitions outlined by the authors. Given the complexity of false information across the digital landscape, our review reveals a lack of consensus regarding definitions of these concepts.
Summary of Realized Interventions
Of the 227 articles we reviewed, fewer than 10% formally assessed their reported interventions, programs, or curricula; neither did we find consistent pedagogical or evaluative approaches to mis/disinformation literacy. However, various interventions shared modes of delivery; we organize and report on these accordingly (see Figure 5).

Figure 5. Breakdown of the intervention formats employed by studies that described and reported evaluations or lessons learned from mis/disinformation literacy interventions.
Course-Based InterventionsSeveral studies (n = 9) discussed course-based interventions focused on teaching news or digital information literacy skills. For example, Cilella (2019) reported on a series of library-based workshops where a librarian teaches the history of fake news, examines people’s motivations for producing and sharing fake news, and runs an activity called “Real or Fake?.” The activity helped users gain traction and raise awareness about the difficulty of determining the validity of content online.
Murrock et al. (2018) described their Learn-to-Discern curriculum for undergraduate students, where they defined phenomena like propaganda, fake news, and manipulation, and discussed media ownership and types of media. Through practical exercises, students analyzed media using debunking tools and identifying markers of fake or manipulated content and propaganda such as hate speech and stereotypes. One month after the training, 80% to 90% of them reported using the news literacy skills they learned, and the majority retained cross-checking behavior 18 months after the training.
Two studies evaluated Massive Open Online Courses (MOOCs). One MOOC focused on how the media works and provided instruction on how to be “more active and informed media users” (Roschke, 2018, p. 7). The second incorporated a digital health literacy component that sought to improve students’ ability to evaluate healthcare information (Blakemore et al., 2020).
Hobbs et al. (2018) described a virtual knowledge exchange between American and German undergraduate students that focused on discussions and analysis of political propaganda. The program consisted of five learning experiences in which students discussed their previous experiences learning about propaganda, judged examples of international propaganda as harmful or beneficial, analyzed and annotated propaganda videos, and compared political campaign videos from German and American contexts. Students gained greater awareness of the importance of cultural specificity and context of the propaganda as well as its emotional potency (Hobbs et al., 2018).
Hanz and Kingsland (2020) provided a thorough description of their recurring workshop on fake news offered initially to international high school students and subsequently to undergraduate and graduate students, faculty, staff, and alumni at McGill University, conducted 19 times over 2 years and adapted throughout. It included presentations and interactive discussions on history of fake news, forms of journalistic bias, tips to recognize photo alterations, Google search techniques, and analyzing news articles that cite academic articles. Interactive components included sharing their own examples of fake news, and reflecting on personal bias. Takeaways included the need to provide a list of websites that debunk fake news during activities in which participants judge the veracity of information and to ensure that websites/resources provided do not contain misleading, false, or triggering content.
Colglazier (2017) described the high school history course he teaches and the lessons learned over time. He highlights the importance of asking questions rather than simply lecturing. His approach included teaching and modeling to students how to discern the source of information by cross-checking information with other sites (lateral reading), analyzing information, and viewing online search results of pages beyond the first.
Jones (2018) described a lesson focused on deconstructing a news article that referenced an unpublished paper by a Harvard scholar on the policing and targeting of Black people in the USA. Students were assigned a New York Times article to read along with supplementary study questions and basic background information about the article’s topic of police brutality as context, to consider news framing and author credibility. The second part of the lesson involved class discussion regarding information reliability and limitations of research methodologies.
In Walton and colleagues’ (2018) UK-based study on information discernment, A-level students identified three information sources they used recently, indicating their level of trust and reasons for choosing these sources. In small group workshops (fewer than seven participants), groups designed posters on what constitutes good and bad sources. Follow-up interviews with seven students indicated that the sessions encouraged students to rely more on books and less on Wikipedia as their only source. Interviews with the students, teachers and librarians confirmed that students showed a greater sense of skepticism about information, and displayed improved questioning behavior about source credibility.
Public EventsThree studies provided details about public events on disinformation and journalism. Rush (2018) and de los Santos et al. (2018) described panel events in which various professionals (namely professors, TV and radio journalists, museum leaders, graduate students) discussed the history and challenges of fake news, how it goes viral, and how to judge the reliability of news and consume it responsibly. Participants in de los Santos et al.’s (2018) study found value in the diverse experts present, allowing participants to pose questions about journalistic practices.
Branstiter et al. (2018) reported on three media literacy activities conducted in a university setting, to complement their media literacy library guides. Activities included a fact-checking party during the final 2016 US presidential debate where students raised flags to indicate statements as being true, false, or red herrings, and a teach-in where faculty gave 10-minute lightning talks about their area of research, including journalism, communication, and women and gender studies. The study found that activities should be planned outside exam time and advertised appealingly to encourage students to attend.
Web-Based InterventionsTwo studies conducted web-based interventions. Tully et al. (2020) tested the effectiveness of news literacy tweets on perceptions of information credibility and news literacy beliefs. The purpose of these tweets was to “mitigate the impact of exposure to misinformation about two health issues” and “boost people’s perceptions of their own media literacy and media literacy’s value to society broadly” (Tully et al., 2020, p. 23). They found that while news literacy messages can affect people’s perception of message credibility, viewing such messages once is not sufficient. Campaigns should include multiple messages and they should be tailored to the context of the information.
Bonnet and Sellers (2020) described an online, quiz-based activity in which participants received a quiz about COVID-19 for 5 days, and “scrutinized memes on social media, doctors’ credentials, news stories, treatment options, and research about the virus” in order to determine its credibility, trustworthiness, and accuracy (p. 2). After completing the quiz, participants received extensive feedback on how to evaluate and further research each day’s topic. Participants found the quiz fun, educational, and helpful in raising awareness about media literacy challenges; as well, they recommended offering multiple answer options on certain questions instead of only one, as some information could be labeled as both “valid” and “controversial.”
Game-Based InterventionsThree game-based interventions were present in our dataset; two focused on information reliability and validity, and another on role-playing as a fake news producer to build awareness of media deception. The former two games, MAthE (Katsaounidou et al., 2019) and Trustme! (Yang et al., 2021) both contributed positively to participants’ ability to evaluate information or news online. However, Yang et al. (2021) found that their Trustme! game did not enhance skepticism, though it did improve information discernment skills. After playing Maertens et al. (2021) game, The Bad News Game, participants found fake news headlines significantly less reliable than before playing it. However, authors cautioned that rating reliability does not necessarily reveal participants’ beliefs regarding news, recommending that future studies should determine whether participants still believed information regardless of reliability assessment.
Visual ResourcesFive articles reported on interventions that tested the effects of visual resources (infographic and videos) on various indicators of media literacy. Domgaard and Park (2021) randomized participants into three groups to view either an infographic that had tips on finding fake news (infographic condition), a document that contained the text of the infographic (text-only condition), or a prompt ushering participants to press “next” (control group). They found most users had trouble verifying misinformation about vaccines, but that participants in the infographic condition were significantly better at doing so than text-only and control groups, showing lower trust in the false news articles than the control group. These results suggest that “visual cues can positively affect cognitive processing during the verification of vaccine news articles . . . and allowed participants for better retention of news literacy skill implementation while reading vaccine news articles” (p. 982).
Lewandowsky and Yesilada (2021) had participants watch either “inoculation” videos that described common rhetorical markers found in Islamophobic or radical-Islamist disinformation (e.g., making hasty generalizations, evoking emotion/using emotional language with moral undertones, and polarization) or a control video on bitcoin. This video was followed with another containing either Islamophobic or radical-Islamist content. They found that the participants who watched the inoculation video perceived the second video to be less reliable than did control group participants, indicated less agreement with the content of the video, and were less likely to share it.
Vraga et al. (2021) explored the effects of Facebook user corrections of sunscreen-related misinformation, and investigated whether watching a news literacy video before watching videos that either promote or share misinformation about sunscreen would enhance the effects of the user correction. The news literacy video highlighted individual fact-checking such as source evaluation, considering intent, and looking for evidence. They found that a few corrections may not be able to strengthen beliefs to the point before exposure to misinformation, and that the news literacy video did not inoculate participants against the misinformation. The authors predicted that the perceived credibility of the source (a person identified as a doctor vs. a fictional “health” brand) shapes whether users critically evaluate the source. Alternative literacies, authors suggest, such as health or science literacy might be more relevant than the skills taught in news literacy, and that future research should explore how providing a mixture of literacies can aid people in better identifying and resisting health misinformation.
Alexander and Wood (2019) explore the effects of a satirical news video on students’ engagement with news literacy education as well as its impact on how students critically consume the information in the video. Freshmen students at California State University were shown five clips from satirical news shows like The Daily Show and The Colbert Report that touched on the concepts of plagiarism, authority, commercial bias, ethical use of information, information privacy, media ownership, and bias in journalism. Over 90% of students agreed that satirical news made the class more enjoyable, facilitated their understanding, and encouraged them to be more critical media consumers. The authors warn, however, that the satirical nature of the videos is not always understood and educators should provide context and guided discussion alongside satirical videos.
Finally, Hwang et al. (2021) compared the effects of a general media literacy education video, a deepfake-specific literacy video, and no literacy program on adults’ willingness to share a deep fake video. They found that while seeing a deep fake video enhanced the vividness, credibility, and persuasiveness of misinformation and willingness to share it compared to text-only misinformation, participants who saw the general media literacy educational video were least likely to find deep fake videos as vivid and persuasive. While there was no difference in perceived credibility of the misinformation between the experimental conditions, there was a significant difference between these conditions and no literacy video. These results suggest that an educational video tailored specifically to deepfake videos may not be necessary and that a general media literacy video would be effective at reducing the likelihood of accepting and sharing misinformation.
Recommendations from the Research
We now turn to articles that detail recommendations from existing programing and curriculum as well as reviews and essays that focus on strategies for mis/disinformation literacy pedagogy, highlighting recurrent themes and the most common recommendations and strategies emerging from these sources.
Considering Emotions and Practising MindfulnessWithin the scholarship that addresses the role of emotion (14.9% of total, n =34), the need to understand how our emotions are targeted by news, propaganda, and disinformation via personalized messaging was frequently emphasized. Scholars and practitioners advocate developing awareness of the goals and strategies of targeted, emotion-focused narratives (Alvarez, 2021; Serrano-Puche, 2021; Shumaker, 2019; Sivek, 2018). Attempts to spread disinformation strategically rely on emotionally provocative, memorable content (Jaeger & Taylor, 2021; Serrano-Puche, 2021). Thus, students should be aware of how emotional data is collected and used, and how their emotions are targeted and exploited, and the effect that could have on their online and offline behaviors (Sivek, 2018).
Scholars stress the importance of understanding the ways disinformation exploits identities and amplifies pre-existing divisions in society (Logue, 2020; Shumaker, 2019). This may include becoming more aware of the psychological and emotional tendencies that lead them to engage with or resist information and that shape their information-sharing behaviors (Burkhardt, 2017; Logue, 2020). When individuals recognize that their actions and attitudes are connected to their emotional state, they can more readily recognize how media could affect their emotions (Whiting, 2021).
Mindfulness surfaced as a practice invaluable within our fast-paced media culture and pervasive barrage of emotionally heightened information (n = 7; Berkman, 2021; Canada, 2021; Middaugh, 2019; Ojala, 2019; Sivek, 2018; Tsvetkova, 2017; Wineburg & McGrew, 2019). It can be used to monitor reactions to and help us avoid snap judgments (Berkman, 2021). Sivek (2018) notes how mindfulness is grounded in Buddhist tradition, and suggests that it can promote awareness of when, where, and how we are exposed to news, as well as how we read and process news and information. Users can be encouraged to dedicate a specific portion of their day to consuming the news and to log their emotional reactions in the process. Mindfulness media education integrates small pauses, breaths, moments of reflection, and attention to emotions, feelings, and thoughts. Media literacy programs can encourage “click restraint” (Wineburg & McGrew, 2019) and slow reading to regulate information flow (Tsvetkova, 2017).
Other psychological and emotional competencies that emerged in our review included: self-awareness and self-management (Cronkhite et al., 2020; Logue, 2020; Whiting, 2021), empathy (Berkman, 2021; Friesem, 2018; Logue, 2020), compassion (D’Olimpio, 2021), and skepticism (Arth et al., 2019; Burkhardt, 2017; A. M. Guess et al., 2020; Khan & Idris, 2019; Roschke, 2018; Sullivan, 2019; Vraga & Tully, 2021).
Structural and Historic KnowledgeIn line with critical media literacy and in response to exploitation of cognitive biases and the increasing use of emotional targeting and dataveillance, a number of authors highlighted the importance of teaching about structural and macro-level factors that contribute to the spread of mis/disinformation (n = 14). Learners need to be aware of algorithmic personalization and governance and that algorithms are not neutral but instead reflect the (often economic) intentions and goals of the programmer and the platform (Cohen, 2018; Dixon, 2021; Friesem, 2018; Hobbs, 2020). Many suggested teaching about the economics of the news and social media industries in addition to the influence of advertising profits on the design and function of algorithms, social media platforms, and news production (Alcolea-Díaz et al., 2020; Damasceno, 2021; De Abreu, 2021; Fielding, 2019; Friesem, 2018; Manfra & Holmes, 2018; Roquet, 2019).
Several articles recommended teaching about the history of fake news (n = 5), giving students a deeper and broader understanding of its techniques and goals, and how and why it circulates (Spratt & Agosto, 2017). Educators and librarians may use news articles from different historical contexts, as a springboard for exploring similar and/or differing themes and techniques in the present (LaPierre, 2020).
Some authors (n = 6) indicated that media literacy should be intentionally civic and political (Arth et al., 2019; Berkman, 2021; Fister, 2021; Friesem, 2018; Middaugh, 2019; Mihailidis & Viotty, 2017), emphasizing media literacy’s aim as empowering learners as active citizens. Arth et al. (2019) recommended that media literacy skills be repositioned as a mode of civic participation rather than a skill for critically analyzing individual texts. Finally, Fister (2021) mentions that we should frame media literacy through a lens of democracy, rather than taking a partisan position. This is in line with several other authors who encourage perspective taking and empathy in the consumption of media and social dialog (Berkman, 2021; Friesem, 2018).
Lateral Reading and the Research and Scientific ProcessA significant number of articles (n = 12) suggested teaching lateral reading: searching for information about a source using external resources external to evaluate credibility (Faix, 2018; Miller, 2018). Lateral reading helps users understand how the Internet and search engines are structured and how to make searching and navigating effective and efficient (Wineburg & McGrew, 2019). As opposed to checklists that tend to focus on the singular text in isolation, lateral reading encourages visiting other websites to verify information (Faix, 2018; Fielding, 2019; Manfra & Holmes, 2020; Wineburg & McGrew, 2019).
Damasceno (2021) suggested using reflection questions such as “what do I know about the source,” or “if this content is true, what else would be true?” Tynes et al. (2021) suggested that lateral reading alone is not enough, and should be paired with critical reading so students understand how searches yield biased results. Overall, lateral reading is frequently suggested as it attends to the complexity of the fake news context (Sullivan, 2019).
Educators and librarians also suggested teaching research skills (n = 5). Sorrell (2019) introduced ways to incorporate Indigenous knowledge in information literacy where students engage in the research stages of “thinking” (choosing, a research topic), “planning” (developing research strategies), “life” (application of findings), and “assurance” (ensuring information/knowledge is responsibly accessed and utilized). The confusion around COVID-19 highlighted the need for greater awareness of scientific and research methods, including scientific consensus processes (Berkman, 2021; Linvill, 2019). Vraga et al. (2020) suggested that increasing general public knowledge of the scientific process “may facilitate acceptance of evolving recommendations. . . without undermining trust in scientists and health professionals” (p. 474; also see Badke, 2020).
Fact-CheckingFact-checking interventions continue to be used to combat the belief in and spread of disinformation through the flagging of (potentially) incorrect information or providing expert corrections at the point of contact between a user and online content (Ziemer & Rothmund, 2024). Indeed, many have deemed fact-checking as “an essential skill for staying informed” (Batchelor, 2017, p. 144) and a host of articles indicated that educators and librarians are increasingly compiling lists of automated fact-checking sites to aid students in detecting false and biased information (n = 10). However, if a fact-checking intervention is not available, adults should have the ability to assess the validity of information themselves.
There is consensus on the most reliable fact-checking sites, which include: Factcheck.org, run by the Annenberg Public Policy Center; Politifact.com, run by The Tampa Bay Times; and Snopes.com (Batchelor, 2017; Cilella, 2019; De Abreu, 2021; Faix, 2018; “Four Questions for Frank Baker”, 2016; Jacobson, 2017). In a review of 10 fact-checking sites, Mallon (2018) also recommended Factcheck.org and Allsides.com, as well as games like Factitious and Bad News. Browser extensions such as Media Bias Fact Check, Fake News Alert, and B.S. Detector are also suggested to help flag fake or suspicious information while searching on the web (Wade & Hornick, 2018). When considering strategies for implementing fact-checking sites in the classroom, Faix (2018) suggested beginning with a trending topic rather than one toward which users may already have a bias about.
Collaborative Learning and Active ParticipationNumerous studies emphasized the importance of collaborative learning and active participation using discussion-based pedagogies as opposed to teacher-directed or lecture-based interventions (n = 10). This includes having students debate ethical issues about what counts as propaganda (Heller, 2021), group assignments and peer review to encourage collaborative problem-solving (Kaufman, 2021), class discussions about source credibility and trustworthiness (Glisson, 2019; Hobbs, 2017a; Jones, 2018), and exploring misinformation through virtual reality (Young et al., 2021). Discussion-based interventions help students build confidence while thinking critically and deeply about media texts (Jones, 2018). While attempts to correct false information can lead to backfire effects and resistance from learners, including learners as active participants can give them more agency and help them “retain information more effectively” (Glisson, 2019, p. 477; Kaufman, 2021). Active learning approaches encourage learners to consider their role as civic participants, actively engaging in media in more complex ways that go beyond fact-checking (Manfra & Holmes, 2018).
Visual Literacy StrategiesStudies (n = 6) revealed the need for visual literacy skills to respond to a complex media ecosystem where images are highly vulnerable to distortion. Visual thinking strategies encourage students to slow down and question images, trace the source of a photograph, and legitimize URLs (Snelling, 2019). In their modules for teaching about fake news, librarians include the skills required to detect image manipulation, such as reverse image searching (Dahri & Richard, 2018). Swerzenski (2021) advocated expanding students’ visual literacy skills to include photo editing to ensure understanding how airbrushing, layers, and filters shape both perceptions of images and culture at large. Users may also consider the affordances and risks of using images or memes to accompany an article or topic and how these visuals affect our understanding of the story (Hobbs, 2017a; Wade & Hornick, 2018). To keep up with the increasing circulation of fake visual content, educators can provide current and relevant examples of manipulated visual material and identify techniques (Walker, 2019).
Student- and Culturally-Centered ApproachesStudies (n = 6) highlighted the importance and need for media literacy interventions being student-centered and tailored to the needs of the target individuals (Auberry, 2018; Brashier & Schacter, 2020; Moore & Hancock, 2020; Mutsvairo & Bebawi, 2019; Rosenzweig, 2017; Samtani, 2019). One size does not fit all, especially across geographic location, age group, learning styles, and social groups. For example, Mutsvairo and Bebawi (2019) note that Western conceptualizations of fake news do not “resonate with local contexts in Africa and the Middle East” (p. 147), and urge educators to situate understandings of fake news within the regions and cultures in which they manifest. For the older adult population, Brashier and Schacter (2020) stated that interventions should meet the shifting goals of this population while Moore and Hancock (2020) suggested that programs should provide resources for fact-checking, since retired older adults may have more time to engage in fact-checking and be more civically and politically minded than younger people. Finally, Samtani (2019) notes that immigrants tend to be the target of many disinformation campaigns; for media literacy interventions to have the desired effect, immigrants’ needs (e.g., language, media diet) and perceptions of the media and its role in society must be considered.
Debates in the Literature
Despite unanimous concern regarding the spread of false information, many debates arose regarding how to best address this concern given the modern challenges we are facing in the age of social media and Web 2.0. This section highlights key areas of contention that emerged in the literature.
Checklist ApproachesWe found that educational programs and media literacy guides often rely on information evaluation frameworks, usually in the form of checklists, to guide learners to assess the credibility and reliability of media content and authors. A frequently recommended framework is the CRAAP Test (currency, relevance, authority, accuracy, purpose; California State University, Chico, 2010). The CRAAP test was utilized and promoted in Canada (Hanz & Kingsland, 2020), Pakistan (Naeem & Bhatti, 2020), the UK (Clough & Closier, 2018), and Ireland (De Paor & Heravi, 2020). In South Africa, 44 out 48 of the librarian guides addressing disinformation contained links to evaluation tools such as the CRAAP test and “How to Spot Fake News” (Bangani, 2021). The same trend existed in the US, where all 21 librarian guides evaluated suggested checklist approaches to detecting fake news or evaluating news sources (Lim, 2020).
In response to contemporary threats in our media ecosystem and criticisms of the CRAAP Test’s inability to address them, some authors suggested either adaptations or novel frameworks. One adaptation was the “CRAAP-based” RADAR framework, which focused on evaluating rationale, authority, date, accuracy, and relevance (Neely-Sardon & Tignor, 2018). Other proposed checklists include the IMVA/IN framework (independent, multiple, verify, authoritative/informed, named), SIFT (stop, investigate the source, find trusted coverage, and trace claims; Ojala, 2019), and CARS (credibility, accuracy, reasonableness, support; Gardner, 2017; Jacobson, 2017).
A third group of scholars challenged the effectiveness of checklists and suggested more updated and nuanced approaches (n = 12; 5.3%; for example, Feekery & Jeffrey, 2019; Hodgin & Kahne, 2018). Checklists were criticized as being outdated, ineffective, and unrealistic in the context of a fast-paced “infodemic” (McGrew et al., 2017; Sullivan, 2019). Others expressed concern that the checklist approach “bypasses the need for critical thinking” (Saunders & Budd, 2020, p. 2; Johnson, 2018), “flattening” complex decision-making processes into a set of heuristics (Beene & Greer, 2021, p. 6), and limiting opportunities for open-ended, inductive, and exploratory approaches to text (Shenton, 2021).
AuthorityWhat counts as authoritative and credible information if there is no agreement about expertise and intent? How can educators teach both the importance of approaching sources critically while also retaining trust in and respect for field professionals? These questions were described as some of “the biggest challenges” facing educators and librarians (Badke, 2020, p. 37; Clough & Closier, 2018; De Paor & Heravi, 2020; Lim, 2020; Saunders & Budd, 2020; Smith, 2017).
Hobbs (2017b) highlighted how questions of authority are more complex given “new forms” of authority (e.g., social media influencers). Scholars showcased differing opinions regarding the “Authority is Constructed and Contextual” frame from the Association of College and Research Libraries (ACRL) Framework, updated in 2016. Traditional instruction on authority focused on author credentials with a preference for scholarly and government publishers, privileging institutional knowledge dominated by demographics. The new approach to the authority frame recognizes different types of authority, understands “lived experience as a particular kind of authority,” and acknowledges that authoritative information can be presented traditionally or untraditionally, such as through oral storytelling (Saunders & Budd, 2020, p. 3).
Others shared concerns that the frame does not adequately address today’s “post-truth” reality (Lynch & Hunter, 2020). Saunders and Budd (2020) stated that the frame goes too far in challenging traditional indicators of authority, encouraging students to reject authoritative sources and consider more “unlikely” sources. Additionally, understandings of authority that are too open-ended leave the receiver to determine the trustworthiness of any piece of information, leading to calls to return to a world in which “we trust the expertise of those who know” (Badke, 2020, p. 38).
SkepticismDebates regarding evaluation of authority led to further questions regarding the value of “skepticism.” Some authors strongly advocated skepticism as a quality critical for rejecting mis/disinformation (Sullivan, 2019) and an effective way to “combat the biases and psychological preferences built into our brains, at least long enough to consider alternatives” (Burkhardt, 2017, p. 26). Vraga and Tully (2021) found that those who are more news literate are more skeptical of social media information quality.
However, several scholars noted the challenge of encouraging skepticism without creating cynicism and distrust of all information (Albert et al., 2020). Skepticism involves doubt and asking questions, skills that are described as necessary for participatory democracy, while cynicism involves distrust and “creates disengagement and disillusionment” (Vraga & Tully, 2021, p. 154). For other scholars, skepticism comes at the expense of distrust in government (Albert et al., 2020) and mainstream news (A. M. Guess et al., 2020; Vraga & Tully, 2021). Albert et al. (2020) even described skepticism as a “deterrent” (p. 34), and suggested educators and librarians instead “counter student skepticism” (p. 36).
The risks associated with skepticism led some scholars to advocate a balanced approach that encouraged verification and analysis of credibility and content, while maintaining a sense of trust. This “healthy skepticism” approach encourages individuals to understand their participatory role and responsibility in sharing problematic information (Khan & Idris, 2019; Roschke, 2018). To avoid cynicism, individuals must not feel overwhelmed by information choices and must recognize the value of media literacy in a democratic society (Vraga & Tully, 2021).
ResponsibilityAcross this review, divergent perspectives about who is responsible and accountable for the health of the information and media environments appeared to influence the design and approach of the interventions. The extent to which users are positioned as individually responsible for identifying disinformation varies. Some interventions helped participants to avoid disinformation consumption, often by relying on fact-checking and checklist frameworks (Dixon, 2021; Wade & Hornick, 2018), while others taught participants to prevent the spread and sharing of disinformation by emphasizing media literacy as a self-reflective practice (Krutkowski et al., 2020; Lynch & Hunter, 2020; Roquet, 2019).
While most media literacy interventions focused on strategies that can be employed by individuals, others invoked the role of governments, technology companies, policymaking, and regulation (Gilchrist, 2018; Hanz & Kingsland, 2020). Faix (2018) notes that while media literacy interventions based on source evaluation hold individual users responsible for seeking credible information without addressing the agents who create and publish disinformation, this burden of individual responsibility is also a necessity. Given that the profitability and pervasiveness of disinformation is unlikely to be eradicated, individuals need to be empowered to make critical and informed decisions of their own.
Addressing the PoliticalAnother prominent debate revolved around the degree to which the political aspects of mis/disinformation in media literacy should be addressed, especially given the increased concern regarding fake news post-2016. The term “fake news” was itself criticized as being politically laden given that it often serves to “amplify a right-wing political agenda to undermine the credibility of centrist and center-left media organizations” (Head et al., 2018, p. 41). One group of scholars advocated rejecting the stance of neutrality and instead actively teaching political topics (e.g., elections, policies, and conspiracy theories; Fister, 2021; Hobbs, 2017a; Jaeger & Taylor, 2021). Alvarez (2021) called upon libraries to take a proactive political stance by adhering to diversity, equity, and inclusion practices among staff, while also partnering with governments, nongovernmental organizations, civil society, and community groups such as local task forces and boards. While the politically motivated nature of disinformation is broadly highlighted within these studies, specific ideologies or actors are not necessarily mentioned.
Another group of scholars recommended avoiding explicit political discussions so as to prevent further polarization or backlash. Young et al. (2021) stated that communities predicated on disinformation offer emotional and social affirmation to members, and cannot be dismantled by cold truths. Instead, programing must help people to build new communities based on truth, most effectively implemented by a broad approach to literacy. Similarly, Ireland (2017) encouraged media literacy training that teaches about elements of disinformation within general entertainment media to make programing both personally relevant and broadly inclusive. Dar (2021) forwarded a “devil’s advocate” approach, whereby various perspectives to news events are considered without alienating learners of diverse political views.
Discussion
The aim of this essay is to guide future research and programing through a review of research, published between 2016 and 2022, on effective promotion of mis/disinformation literacy among adult populations. Ours joins several other reviews and studies conducted during a similar timeframe that attempt to enhance adult mis/disinformation literacy practice and research, indicating the timeliness and necessity of such investigation (Droog et al., 2024; Dumitru et al., 2022; Frau-Meigs, 2022; Kanozia et al., 2022; Wright et al., 2023; Ziemer & Rothmund, 2024). We discovered a significant increase in the number of publications in 2017, indicating the spike in interest in mis/disinformation-related media literacy. There was a steady increase in publications between 2017 and 2021, with a peak in 2020, a trend supported by Kanozia et al. (2022) who found a similar increase between 2017 and 2020.
We found that published interventions were diverse in their mode of delivery and included: offline and online formal education-based training; public events often organized by librarians, web-based learning activities, social media messaging, games, and visual resources such as videos and infographics. Relatively few interventions were formally evaluated and success was measured through a variety of outcomes. The largest number of evaluated interventions were those conducted in formal education settings targeting undergraduate and some upper high school students (37.4%). Those that discussed their intervention’s effectiveness often reported positive changes among students/participants (e.g., Blakemore et al., 2020; Lewandowsky & Yesilada, 2021; Murrock et al., 2018); however, it was rare that learners were assessed over time.
The majority of interventions in our review focused on news or information literacy (as opposed to advertising or digital literacies; e.g., LaPierre, 2020; Maertens et al., 2021; Neely-Sardon & Tignor, 2018). Many interventions called for learners to analyze texts or videos, engage in discussions with peers and educators, and/or pose questions to experts in the context of panel discussions (e.g., de los Santos et al., 2018; Domgaard & Park, 2021; Hobbs et al., 2018). They also incorporated discussions about and use of checklists, such as the CRAAP test, but we note significant debate across the literature regarding the usefulness of checklists, with some criticizing them as outdated and even hindering critical thinking. Lateral reading has been suggested as a useful alternative or addition to checklists.
Many of the recommendations from experts and scholars within our review aligned with components and recommendations of intervention reports; however, some recommendations stood out as novel and understudied, namely mindfulness strategies and the focus on developing emotional reflexivity during information exposure. Such strategies may be useful in monitoring and regulating affective reactions within the modern context of information anxiety.
Collaboration and active participation of learners emerged as key components, taking the form of debates, class discussions, and group assignments. This aligns with calls for recognizing media literacy as a tool for civic participation, helping learners to see themselves as engaged and active civic participants.
Gaps and Recommendations for Research
Perhaps most starkly, our review shows a significant gap in evaluated research relevant to mis/disinformation literacy for adult and older adult populations. While there were studies reporting on interventions held in libraries and universities, online, and through gaming platforms or various visual means, the divergent approaches and evaluation methods limit any evidence-based recommendations. Although many articles provide “lessons learned” or suggested recommendations, most interventions did not include a control or comparison group and newer recommendations were not always substantiated with evidence or evaluation. The growing concern over the spread of false information makes it imperative to enhance our understanding of ways to provide effective mis/disinformation literacy to adults. This can be achieved through more experimental and field research but also through systematic evaluations of existing programs and newer recommendations (e.g., mindfulness, emotional regulation).
Another significant gap revealed by our review is the lack of studies/programing targeting adult and older adult populations and their needs and abilities outside of formal education. Indeed, the overrepresentation of college students as the primary focus across these articles demonstrates a clear limitation in the literature on mis/disinformation literacy. This is concerning given that older adults in particular are disproportionately targeted by disinformation online given not infrequent lack of necessary requisite digital media skills. They also have more difficulty detecting deception given that interpersonal trust increases with age (Brashier & Schacter, 2020). Older adults may also have unique affordances: retired adults often have more time and may be more inclined to effectively fact-check (Moore & Hancock, 2020). Droog et al. (2024) reviewed experimental media literacy studies published between 2018 and 2022 and found that although many of the studies targeted general adult populations, there were inconsistencies in reporting age, making it difficult to generalize recommendations for children and the elderly. Future studies should examine the needs and skills of adult populations, and on this basis determine what components to include in programing, where programing should be held (e.g., online vs. in-person), and how best to communicate mis/disinformation literacy education. Studies should also be intentional and clear in reporting user age and other consequential demographic and psychological factors so that practitioners can be confident in applying research to practice.
While some authors provided recommendations for how to tackle conspiracy theories (e.g., Beene & Greer, 2021; Hobbs, 2017a), research regarding how to discuss potentially sensitive topics among adults (e.g., conspiracy theories, hate and free speech, social justice issues) was minimal. A notable exception article is Beene and Greer’s (2021), which provided a thorough discussion of strategies for tackling conspiracy thinking, taking the emotional nature of conspiracies into account. More research is needed on this topic, as without proper training and knowledge on how to address difficult conversations, educators may lack the confidence and skills to tackle them and even subsequently avoid doing so.
The debates regarding definitions and classifications of different forms of false, misleading, and manipulated information are ongoing; however, the lack of an accepted vocabulary in this context adds an additional challenge to the production of recommendations for effective media education practices. Consensus and delineation of the phenomena in the media landscape is crucial for researchers and practitioners to study and evaluate media education interventions and programing and present generalizable recommendations. However, given the rapid changes and evolutions in the media landscape, this process needs to be dynamic, but nonetheless well-considered.
Our review made it clear that what is required is not decontextualized media literacy strategies but rather an understanding of the myriad and complex components of our media landscape, including algorithms and economic, historical, political, psychological, and cultural factors that shape what content is produced and disseminated through journalism, social media, and other media forms. Educators are encouraged to take into account the increasingly visual culture of media and incorporate lessons on how to spot or evaluate visual and auditory manipulations (e.g., deepfakes, manipulated images). They should also tailor content and the mode of delivery to the specific needs of learners (language, culture, geographic location, age, media use). Without this, lessons may backfire or be ineffective, particularly if irrelevant to the learner and their socio-cultural and political context.
Limitations
This review is not without limitations. While it provides significant insight into the adult mis/disinformation-based media literacy education literature since 2016, media literacy programing and concerns about propaganda and the spread of false information are not modern phenomena, and studies/programing published prior to 2016 may provide an even more comprehensive picture of effective ways to design programs. Nonetheless, the media landscape is evolving quickly and it is imperative that we determine how to effectively teach adults to productively engage in mis/disinformation literacy. A second limitation is the inclusion of articles published only in English, imposing a predominantly Western-centric lens, which may limit generalizability of findings and recommendations. Third, our review criteria was inclusive of studies that targeted adults of all ages but also upper high school students, as these studies may help inform non-formal education programing for adults. However, the lifestyle, capabilities, motivations, and levels of engagement and familiarity with digital media on the part of the younger demographic is distinct from those of mid-aged and older adults, potentially requiring different approaches to programing. Future studies may benefit from delineating effective programing for young, middle-aged, and older adults. Fourth, we included articles that varied in type, namely experimental and field studies, reviews, essays, and opinion pieces. Given the nature of a scoping review, evaluating the quality of these articles and the methods used in the interventions were not within the purview or goals of the review. Rather, our aim was to describe the nature of the interventions being investigated and implemented and what practitioners and experts are recommending. As the literature develops, systematic and meta-analytical reviews are needed to provide robust recommendations for mis/disinformation literacy programing. Given publishing lag times, future reviews should also conduct extensive and systematic exploration of all gray literature to ensure inclusion of the most up-to-date material. Finally, given our research focus on literature based in the social sciences and education, we ran our search in discipline-specific databases and not in general databases such as Web of Science, Scopus or Google Scholar. While our chosen databases are some of the largest in their field and were approved by specialist librarians, Web of Science and/or Scopus likely cast a wider net. Future research could build on our review by widening the scope of the search to such databases.
Conclusion
Ultimately, the gaps in adult media literacy demonstrate the need for a conceptualization of mis/disinformation literacy as an integrated, lifelong practice. It should extend beyond traditional curricula and provide grounded, practical applicability to everyday life for individuals across the lifespan. Given the rapid evolution of the media landscape, approaches need to be similarly dynamic and adaptive. For this to become reality, continued research and practical, evidence-based guidelines, recommendations, and resources need to be in place to support the educators and librarians on the ground. This article offers a step in this direction, reviewing recent studies and recommendations on effective ways to educate adults about false information and empower them to be active, critical readers of news and information in our fast-changing media landscape.

16 Theories of public opinion
Abstract: While the issue of citizen competency has vexed scholars throughout
history, the modern concepts of a mass public and mass media are relatively new.
Beginning with the seminal works of Lippmann and Dewey, we chart the evolving
theories of public opinion, from the "hypodermic needle" model of the early twentieth century to the more psychologically oriented approach to media effects of
today. We argue that in addition to understanding how audiences process media
content, theories of public opinion must account for how media content is constructed and disseminated, which is complicated by the ever-changing nature of
our media landscape.
Keywords: Public opinion, mass media, gatekeeping, media effects
1 Introduction
Popular discourse about public opinion tends to revolve around key issues of the
day. Citizens bemusedly ask themselves how the public comes to hold a particular
view on a given issue. Voters anticipate how political candidates will strategize
and frame an issue to garner the most support possible. And individuals consume
hews stories and read blogs on the internet, later taking advantage of comment
boxes to share their perspectives.
Academic endeavors related to public opinion focus on the same issues. They
examine the process by which information gets presented, how citizens learn about
issues, and the effects of this information on attitudes, thoughts, and behaviors.
However, scholarship on public opinion is not only empirical in nature: research
ih this area is undergirded by a strong set of normative assumptions. For example,
Who constitutes the public? What should the members of an ideal citizenry know
about politics and how engaged should they be in the political process? Should
an 1pinion grounded in emotion carry as much weight as an opinion based on
information?
In studying the aforementioned processes, public opinion scholars inextricably
lihk public opinion to the functioning of democratic SOCiety.! Given this view of public

This view of public opinion as a form of social control has allowed researchers to study public

Although the term "public opinion" was not coined until the mid-1700s (see Peters
1995 for a review), our point of departure is the early twentieth-century intellectual
debate between Walter Lippmann and John Dewey, whose differences in perspective
reflected longstanding debates and would trickle down through the decades to create
a rich corpus of literature. The Lippmann-Dewey debate is critical as its key concerns
are reflected in the various theories of public opinion, all of which involve media

over the past century, and end with a discussion of how these theories need to be
revisited in light of an increasingly technologically oriented media environment.
2 Early twentieth-century perspectives
2.1 Views of the public: Lippmann vs. Dewey
From ancient Greece onward, citizen competence has been at the heart of many
debates about the public. Questions about whether citizens were sufficiently
knowledgeable to rule or whether governance should be left to Plato's philosopher
Idngs have emerged consistently over the years. Indeed, this remained the crux of
how public intellectual Walter Lippmann and theorist John Dewey saw the public
in the early 1900s.
Lippmann, in his oft-cited books Public Opinion (1922) and The Phantom Public
(1925), painted a pejorative portrait of the public - one that was unable to process
information deeply or to behave rationally. In Public Opinion, Lippmann relied on
the allegory of the cave, from Book VII of Plato's The Republic. In this story, a
group of men has been chained together in a cave since childhood. The chains
prevent them from moving their legs or turning their heads; consequently, they
are able to see only that which passes before them. And because a fire as well as
the mouth of the cave are behind them, the chained men see nothing but the
shadows cast upon the wall of the cave as others might walk by. The allegory
ends, "And if they were able to talk with one another, would they not suppose
that they were naming what was actually before them?"
Lippmann presented another allegory in Public Opinion, one set in 1914 at the
onset of the Great War. Englishmen, Frenchmen, and Germans lived on an island,
sufficiently remote that it received mail once every two months. When the mail
arrived in mid-September 1914, they learned how their respective countries had
been engaged in hostilities. "For six strange weeks they had acted as if they were 
Theories of public opinion - 291
friends, when in fact they were enemies" (Lippmann 1922: 3). Lippmann used these
two examples to illustrate how indirectly citizens know the environment in which
they live. Acknowledging how "the real environment is altogether too big, too complex, and too fleeting for direct acquaintance," he contended that citizens were
"not equipped to deal with so much subtlety, so much variety, so many permutations and combinations" (16). As a result, citizens are forced to rely on what they
can to create for themselves trustworthy pictures of the world beyond their reach.
Naturally, the mass media playa critical role in the construction of these pictures.
As much as citizens can use the media to learn about their unseen lifespace,
they inherently cannot process mediated information fully. Lippmann (1922: 30)
identified several factors as limiting access to the facts:
They are the artificial censorships, the limitations of social contact, the comparatively meager
time available in each day for paying attention to public affairs, the distortion arising because
events have to be compressed into very short messages, the difficulty of making a small
vocabulary express a complicated world, and finally the fear of facing those facts which would
seem to threaten the established routine of men's lives.
Hence, his skepticism that citizens were able to contribute significan.t1y to democratic processes.
Just as Aristotle's view of the public was antithetical to Plato's, Lippmann's
perspective generated much response, most notably from philosopher and education reformer John Dewey, who expressed considerably greater optimism regarding
the populace. Like Lippmann, he recognized that citizens were imperfect, but his
Aristotelean perspective emphasized the supremacy of public opinion as the best
safeguard to democracy (Bullert 1983). Is there potential to strengthen our citizenry, and if so, how? Dewey, in his seminal work Tile Public and its Problems
(1927), argued that to help an entity "largely inchoate and unorganized" (109),
structural changes were needed: "The essential need ... is the improvement of the
methods and conditions of debate, discussion and persuasion. That is the problem
of the public" (208). Indeed, for Dewey, it was necessary to foster "conditions
under which the Great Society may become the Great Community" (147).
Dewey's thinking reflected a profound concern with improving how citizens
learned and how they could reach their fullest potential. In his works (e.g., The
Logic of Inquiry, 1938), he advocated the use of logic, supported application of the
sCientific method, and argued that the use of reasoning should be linked to policy
and social concerns.
Though most reviews of Lippmann and Dewey tend to juxtapose them as
almost diametrically opposite in thought, the two strands of thinking are aligned
With each other. As Sproule (1997: 97) noted, "Their ideas fed a view that the weakminded and dangerously neurotic public could not be trusted to take intelligent
Pdlitical action without formal training, supported by quantitative assessment, in
how to think." Nonetheless, this debate would transcend time and implicate the
Views of how researchers saw citizens being influenced by messages they received.
